highlights.content: # Abundant's Frontier RSI Benchmark: Top AI Models Average Just 34% on Self-Improvement Tasks Ask the average investor what "recursive self-improvement" means and you will get a shrug, followed by "is that a good thing for my Nvidia shares?" The question has suddenly become urgent. Frontier AI models, the most expensive software ever built, score an average of just 34% on a new benchmark designed to measure exactly that capability — whether an AI can improve another AI well enough to do it again, and again, in a loop. That is the central finding from Kevin Lin and Jesse Hu, co-founders of Abundant, who launched Frontier RSI and detailed the results on the MTS podcast. The benchmark is live at frontier-rsi.org, and its top score lands around 34%. "The RSI stuff is just getting started," Lin said. "The top score in our benchmark was like 34% or something like that. So there's still some ways to go." The timing matters. AI-linked stocks have spent the last few weeks selling off, with the S&P 500 sliding into correction territory in November 2026 and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropping 5.3% in a single session as Nvidia and Micron each fell more than 7%. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has publicly modeled a scenario in which AI capital spending fails to pay off. Against that backdrop, the 34% figure is a useful anchor: AI can already do remarkable things, but the self-accelerating loop that justifies much of the hype is nowhere close to closing. ### What "true RSI" actually requires The benchmark began with a definitional argument. Lin and Hu looked at existing "RSI" benchmarks and concluded they were measuring the wrong thing entirely — whether an AI can improve other kinds of AI, other machine-learning models, scientific research, computer-vision problems. That breaks the loop. "In order to have true RSI it needs to have recursion," Hu said. "So basically you need an LLM to improve an LLM so that you can have a recursive loop." His illustration is vivid. If Claude improves Waymo's self-driving stack, there is no mechanism for Waymo to improve Claude back. The improvement happens once and stops. Real RSI requires Claude improving Claude, so that each gain feeds directly into the next round. The obstacle is cost. Training a frontier model like Claude or GPT costs tens to hundreds of millions of dollars by Lin's estimate, money the two-person team does not have. Frontier RSI therefore runs proxy tasks: can a frontier model train and improve smaller models? Lin concedes this is not literally true RSI, but defends it on the grounds that techniques discovered on small models have repeatedly generalized to larger ones. ### The task design: "figure it out on your own" The benchmark splits into four categories of LLM-development work, and every task is framed as an open-ended optimization problem rather than a reproduction exercise. | Category | What the task asks | Example framing | |---|---|---| | Pre-training | Improve a component of the training stack | "Improve the optimizer" with no hint | | Post-training | Train another model to gain a capability | Post-train a model for agentic coding loops (run tests, read errors, edit files, repeat) | | Kernel optimization | Improve a GPU kernel | Open-ended speed/quality optimization | | Inference | Improve inference-side performance | Open-ended optimization | The framing is deliberate. Other benchmarks ask a model to re-implement a known technique, such as the Muon optimizer or FlashAttention, then test whether it reproduced it correctly. Frontier RSI says "improve the model by any means possible" and withholds the method entirely. "If you're a senior researcher somewhere you're not told like re-implement this paper," Lin said. "It's like explore the space of possibilities. I'm not going to tell you how to do it. Just figure it out on your own." Lin and Hu both came from Waymo, and they apply a simulation-and-failure-taxonomy mindset to model evaluation: enumerate edge cases, then detect reward hacks deterministically. The episode is worth the reader's time for the concrete task taxonomy (pre-training, post-training, kernel optimization, inference), the model-by-model results, and the pair's roadmap toward an end-to-end "build an LLM" task. highlights.content: Columns # Global AI industry faces 'Nvidia taper tantrum' As Nvidia tightens its purse strings following scrutiny of its vast AI investments, debt-dependent data center builders and the broader technology market face rising risks. **Ha Hyun-ock** *The author is an editorial writer at the JoongAng Ilbo.* The global AI industry faces an “Nvidia taper tantrum,” as investors fear that the company financing much of the sector could tighten its purse strings following former CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. Interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday that Nvidia would continue supporting and investing in the AI ecosystem but do so more systematically and with rigorous scrutiny, fueling the industry’s anxiety. The concern intensified after news broke of a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into Nvidia’s accounting practices. On Friday, the Nasdaq plunged 5.28 percent, erasing its gains for the year. Previously, customers raised money through their own resources, bonds or bank loans to build data centers and purchase chips. But Nvidia effectively became the AI sector’s central bank, supplying liquidity while assuming some clients’ financing risks; this helped finance infrastructure that would generate demand for Nvidia’s GPUs. Consequently, most of the AI ecosystem became dependent on the company’s support, creating a circular financing structure and rendering the industry vulnerable if its principal financial supporter changes course. Nvidia’s vendor financing extends through equity investments, purchase commitments and guarantees. The Wall Street Journal reported that the company’s investment portfolio, including stakes in companies that buy its chips, exceeds $100 billion, and Nvidia’s regulatory filings showed holdings worth more than $48 billion in eight publicly traded companies at the end of September. Cloud provider CoreWeave, in which Nvidia owns a 10 percent stake, exemplifies this relationship. In September 2025, Nvidia agreed to purchase $6.3 billion in CoreWeave computing capacity. By committing to buy unused capacity at qualifying data centers, the company reduced uncertainty involving its future revenue and helped CoreWeave obtain financing. It also reportedly agreed to guarantee $105 billion for SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary developing a data center to be leased by OpenAI, effectively backing the tenant’s rental obligations. Such deals expose Nvidia to financial obligations tied to whether customers can fill their facilities, generate cash and make payments on time. Nvidia also sought to attract Wall Street capital through an AI financing platform. In August, it announced plans for a $500 billion infrastructure investment consortium, signing memorandums of understanding with Apollo Global Management, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs and KKR. The initiative’s goal was to broaden financing beyond Nvidia itself. But no funds were deployed during its first three months, and reports suggested that one participant considered withdrawing after Huang’s departure. As Nvidia’s era of seemingly unlimited support approaches its end, the circular financing system that it helped construct faces mounting pressure. UBS analyst Tim Arcuri estimated that reduced Nvidia financing could rapidly withdraw more than $50 billion from the market. With borrowing costs already rising, the consequences could spread across the industry. Companies building data centers would face a double squeeze: more expensive financing and fewer guarantees or advance purchase commitments to reassure lenders. Warnings are multiplying. Former U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Gary Gensler told CNN on Nov. 16 that AI was in a bubble and predicted asset repricing and an economic slowdown before November 2028. His concern centers on enormous infrastructure spending, with some estimates putting annual AI infrastructure investment near $800 billion. highlights.content: - Premium Content It takes our newsroom weeks - if not months - to investigate and produce stories for our premium content. You can’t find them anywhere else. # The genAI gold rush puts legacy AI to the test For more than a decade, India-based AI company ShepHertz has built enterprise software powered by machine learning and computer vision. Among its products are facial recognition tools as well as software that monitors remote employees. But the generative AI boom has prompted it to rethink how it builds and sells AI. ShepHertz is in talks to raise US$10 million, its co-founder and CEO Siddhartha Chandurkar tells *Tech in Asia*. The funding will help it invest in GPU resources as it moves into the genAI and agent ecosystem. It will focus on bringing AI capabilities to devices such as drones, vehicles, and home appliances. The shift comes as genAI brings more money and customers into the market. VC investments in genAI firms reached US$35.5 billion in 2025, up from about US$2.8 billion in 2022. Meanwhile, US- and India-headquartered Fractal Analytics says “competition is very high” in the enterprise AI market. The 26-year-old firm was already positioned as an AI player before ChatGPT brought the technology into the mainstream. He says that when the company started, around 20% to 30% of his weekly meetings focused on AI, with discussions largely centered on data. Today, almost every meeting revolves around AI. > All the knowledge of the world is already collected, but how do I make it think more, reason more, and make it special-purpose? “About seven or eight years ago, we were evangelizing AI. Today, everyone knows about it, and we are telling them how to make it feasible,” says Sandeep Dutta, chief product officer of Fractal. For legacy AI companies, the challenge is proving that their expertise, products, and cost efficiencies can give them an edge as the tech becomes more widely accessible. ## Bringing AI closer to users Before generative AI became a multitrillion dollar industry, Fractal used machine learning and predictive analytics to help businesses make decisions. Its models could analyze customer purchase patterns. For instance, they recognized that users who had bought an iPhone and a premium mobile plan were more likely to upgrade to an airline’s premium economy offering. Now, its Customer Genomics solution – which previously used machine learning to build customer profiles from transactions – uses genAI to create personalized marketing messages and images for each customer. Other existing solutions, which use machine learning for managing payments, purchasing, sales, and supply chains, have been upgraded by adding AI agents that can handle tasks with less human intervention. ## Competition, clients, and the cost of AI ## Stay ahead in Asia’s tech landscape This is premium content. AI Agents.content: A personal AI agent runs continuously, keeps memory across sessions, and acts inside your apps. You talk to it in a chat app, by email or by voice. It keeps working after you close the window. The category started small. OpenClaw began in November 2025 as Clawdbot, a weekend project by Peter Steinberger. Twelve months later, Google, OpenAI, Meta and Perplexity all ship their own versions. The products split into 2 camps. Self-hosted agents run on your machine or server and use any model you choose. Managed agents run on a vendor’s cloud VM and come bundled with a subscription. ## **How we ranked them** We scored each agent on 3 axes that matter once an agent holds your inbox and credentials. - **Memory:** what persists, where it is stored, and whether you can read, edit or delete it. - **Security:** default permissions, the isolation boundary, approval gates, and the public incident record. - **Cost:** the subscription price, or token spend plus hosting for self-hosted options. Facts come from vendor documentation, launch posts and independent security research. Prices are US list prices as of November 21, 2026. AI Agents.title: AI agents vs physical AI: How software automation differs from embodied robotics
AI Agents.titleZh: AI agents vs physical AI: How software automation differs from embodied robotics
AI Agents.content: Today’s Artificial intelligence has evolved far beyond simple chatbots that merely answer questions or generate text. Two major branches of autonomous AI now dominate engineering and enterprise roadmaps. AI agents and physical AI. While both are built to pursue goals independently rather than waiting for step-by-step human prompts, they operate in fundamentally different environments. One moves bits across software networks, while the other moves atoms in the real world. Understanding where AI agents end and physical AI begins is essential for engineers, developers, and businesses deciding how to automate digital workflows versus physical operations. ## How AI agents automate digital workflows AI agents, often referred to as agentic AI, are autonomous software systems designed to plan, reason, and execute multi-step tasks inside digital environments. According to IMEC and enterprise software architectures, standard generative models simply respond to a prompt and leave the human user to act on the output. An AI agent takes an overarching objective, breaks it into logical subtasks, accesses external software tools or application programming interfaces (APIs), and carries out the workflow end to end. Under the hood, AI agents typically pair large language models (LLMs) or reasoning models with memory modules, orchestration frameworks, and standardized connectors such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP). ### More from AI and Robotics See All When tasked with resolving a supply-chain delay or debugging a software repository, an AI agent can query databases, write and test code, update enterprise resource planning (ERP) records, and send notifications without continuous human hand-holding. Its inputs are text, code, structured data, and digital signals; its outputs are API calls, file edits, and software transactions. ## How physical AI interacts with the real world Physical AI extends autonomous intelligence out of the cloud and into embodied machines, including humanoid robots, autonomous vehicles, warehouse mobile manipulators, and industrial drones. Rather than processing static text or database rows, physical AI systems must perceive, predict, and act upon continuous, messy real-world physics such as gravity, friction, inertia, and shifting lighting. To operate safely alongside humans, physical AI combines multimodal sensor arrays, cameras, LiDAR, radar, force-torque sensors, and accelerometers with specialized models that map sensor data directly to motor commands. In a 2025 arXiv paper introducing the Cosmos World Foundation Models, NVIDIA researchers detailed how video- and physics-aware foundation models help robots internalize real-world dynamics in simulation before deploying to physical hardware. Unlike digital agents that output text or software commands, physical AI outputs real-time actuator torques, joint trajectories, and navigation paths, often running directly on edge processors to avoid network latency. ## Key engineering differences and failure stakes The clearest distinction between AI agents and physical AI lies in their operating constraints and the cost of errors. An AI agent runs inside deterministic digital infrastructure where actions can often be rolled back, sandboxed, or audited in logs if a model hallucinates or misinterprets an instruction. Physical AI enjoys no such undo button. If a vision-language-action model misjudges the weight of a fragile component or fails to detect a wet factory floor, the result can be a dropped payload, damaged machinery, or injury to nearby workers. Consequently, physical AI requires closed-loop control running at millisecond intervals, strict safety guardrails, and extensive simulation-to-reality (sim-to-real) training to handle unpredictable edge cases that never appear in purely digital workflows. ## Where the two technologies converge Despite their differences, AI agents and physical AI are increasingly deployed together as complementary layers of autonomous operati...

AI Agents.title: Google builds synthetic internet to test AI agents | The Daily Star
AI Agents.titleZh: Google builds synthetic internet to test AI agents | The Daily Star
AI Agents.content: # Google builds synthetic internet to test AI agents Google has developed a synthetic version of the internet, called the ‘mirror dimension’, to train and evaluate artificial intelligence (AI) agents in realistic online environments without exposing real websites and users to potential security risks. The system, developed by Google’s Chrome team, creates thousands of simulated websites that replicate everyday online activities, including shopping, browsing social media, searching for information and completing online transactions. It is designed to help engineers test Chrome’s auto browse feature, which enables AI agents to navigate websites and perform multi-step tasks on behalf of users. According to Google, testing browser-based AI agents on the public internet presents two major challenges: websites constantly change which make results difficult to reproduce, and autonomous agents can cause unintended consequences when given access to real-world services. The mirror dimension addresses these concerns by providing an isolated environment in which every test starts from an identical baseline. The system allows agents to navigate familiar web addresses, such as YouTube, while secretly redirecting their requests to simulated versions of those websites. This helps prevent agents from recognising that they are operating in a testing environment, which could otherwise influence their behaviour. Google has also developed an automated system to build and maintain the simulated websites. It uses specialised AI agents to research website requirements, write code and evaluate the resulting pages for functionality, accessibility and technical errors. Beyond everyday browsing tasks, the environment is designed to test how AI agents respond to cyber threats, particularly indirect prompt injection. Such attacks involve hiding malicious instructions in website content to manipulate an AI agent into taking unauthorised actions. Google said its automated red-teaming pipeline can generate more than 1,000 potential test cases daily for each security engineer, over 30 times the number an individual could produce manually.

LLMs.content: # Abundant's Frontier RSI Benchmark: Top AI Models Average Just 34% on Self-Improvement Tasks Ask the average investor what "recursive self-improvement" means and you will get a shrug, followed by "is that a good thing for my Nvidia shares?" The question has suddenly become urgent. Frontier AI models, the most expensive software ever built, score an average of just 34% on a new benchmark designed to measure exactly that capability — whether an AI can improve another AI well enough to do it again, and again, in a loop. That is the central finding from Kevin Lin and Jesse Hu, co-founders of Abundant, who launched Frontier RSI and detailed the results on the MTS podcast. The benchmark is live at frontier-rsi.org, and its top score lands around 34%. "The RSI stuff is just getting started," Lin said. "The top score in our benchmark was like 34% or something like that. So there's still some ways to go." The timing matters. AI-linked stocks have spent the last few weeks selling off, with the S&P 500 sliding into correction territory in November 2026 and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropping 5.3% in a single session as Nvidia and Micron each fell more than 7%. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has publicly modeled a scenario in which AI capital spending fails to pay off. Against that backdrop, the 34% figure is a useful anchor: AI can already do remarkable things, but the self-accelerating loop that justifies much of the hype is nowhere close to closing. ### What "true RSI" actually requires The benchmark began with a definitional argument. Lin and Hu looked at existing "RSI" benchmarks and concluded they were measuring the wrong thing entirely — whether an AI can improve other kinds of AI, other machine-learning models, scientific research, computer-vision problems. That breaks the loop. "In order to have true RSI it needs to have recursion," Hu said. "So basically you need an LLM to improve an LLM so that you can have a recursive loop." His illustration is vivid. If Claude improves Waymo's self-driving stack, there is no mechanism for Waymo to improve Claude back. The improvement happens once and stops. Real RSI requires Claude improving Claude, so that each gain feeds directly into the next round. The obstacle is cost. Training a frontier model like Claude or GPT costs tens to hundreds of millions of dollars by Lin's estimate, money the two-person team does not have. Frontier RSI therefore runs proxy tasks: can a frontier model train and improve smaller models? Lin concedes this is not literally true RSI, but defends it on the grounds that techniques discovered on small models have repeatedly generalized to larger ones. ### The task design: "figure it out on your own" The benchmark splits into four categories of LLM-development work, and every task is framed as an open-ended optimization problem rather than a reproduction exercise. | Category | What the task asks | Example framing | |---|---|---| | Pre-training | Improve a component of the training stack | "Improve the optimizer" with no hint | | Post-training | Train another model to gain a capability | Post-train a model for agentic coding loops (run tests, read errors, edit files, repeat) | | Kernel optimization | Improve a GPU kernel | Open-ended speed/quality optimization | | Inference | Improve inference-side performance | Open-ended optimization | The framing is deliberate. Other benchmarks ask a model to re-implement a known technique, such as the Muon optimizer or FlashAttention, then test whether it reproduced it correctly. Frontier RSI says "improve the model by any means possible" and withholds the method entirely. "If you're a senior researcher somewhere you're not told like re-implement this paper," Lin said. "It's like explore the space of possibilities. I'm not going to tell you how to do it. Just figure it out on your own." LLMs.content: ## Key Takeaways Kevin Lin and Jesse Hu's Frontier RSI benchmark finds top AI models average just 34% on open-ended self-improvement tasks, with Gemini best at kernel optimization and Claude at post-training. ## Summary Kevin Lin and Jesse Hu, co-founders of Abundant, argue that "true" recursive self-improvement (RSI) means an LLM improving an LLM so the loop can recurse, and that their newly launched Frontier RSI benchmark is the first to test frontier models on that narrow definition. The benchmark's top score is about 34%, which they read as evidence that RSI is early rather than imminent. Most of the conversation covers the benchmark's design choices, how four frontier models split the lead across different LLM-development tasks, and the pair's claim that alignment and capabilities are orthogonal rather than opposed; the title's 34% figure is one data point inside that discussion, and the recent call to ban RSI gets only a brief exchange near the end. Lin and Hu both came from Waymo, and they apply a simulation-and-failure-taxonomy mindset to model evaluation: enumerate edge cases, then detect reward hacks deterministically. The episode is worth the reader's time for the concrete task taxonomy (pre-training, post-training, kernel optimization, inference), the model-by-model results, and the pair's roadmap toward an end-to-end "build an LLM" task. It is thin on hard numbers beyond the 34% headline and the 8-of-27 open-sourced task count. ## Frontier RSI tests whether an LLM can improve an LLM, not AI improving AI in general Lin and Hu built the benchmark because existing "RSI" benchmarks, in their view, measure the wrong thing. Those benchmarks ask whether an AI can improve other kinds of AI — other ML models, scientific research, computer-vision problems — which breaks the recursion. Hu's illustration: if Claude improves Waymo's stack, there is no path for Waymo to improve Claude back. Real RSI requires Claude improving Claude, so that each improvement feeds the next. The practical obstacle is cost. Training a frontier model like Claude or GPT costs, by Lin's estimate, tens to hundreds of millions of dollars, which the team cannot fund. Frontier RSI therefore uses proxy tasks: can a frontier model train and improve smaller models? Lin concedes this is not literally true RSI but defends it on the grounds that techniques discovered on small models have repeatedly generalized to larger ones. The benchmark is organized around four categories of LLM-development work, and every task is framed as an open-ended optimization rather than a reproduction exercise. | Category | What the task asks | Example framing | |---|---|---| | Pre-training | Improve a component of the training stack | "Improve the optimizer" with no hint | | Post-training | Train another model to gain a capability | Post-train a model for agentic coding loops (run tests, read errors, edit files, repeat) | | Kernel optimization | Improve a GPU kernel | Open-ended speed/quality optimization | | Inference | Improve inference-side performance | Open-ended optimization | The framing choice is deliberate. Other benchmarks tell a model to re-implement a known technique such as the Muon optimizer or FlashAttention and then test reproduction. Frontier RSI instead says "improve the model by any means possible" and withholds the method, on the argument that a senior researcher is never handed the paper to reproduce — they are told to explore the space. Lin contrasts this with PostTrainBench, which he says covers grade-school math problems: a toy task rather than a frontier capability. ## The benchmark's top score is about 34%, and no single model leads everywhere The headline result Lin cites is that the best score on Frontier RSI is roughly 34%, which he and Hu treat as evidence that RSI work "is just getting started." LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Strongly Typed Languages Yield Lower Perplexity in Code Completion Across Eighteen Models ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Strongly Typed Languages Yield Lower Perplexity in Code Completion Across Eighteen Models](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/stackrss-featured-22800-bio-7169ce2c156c-1024w.webp) Strongly Typed Languages Yield Lower Perplexity in Code Completion Across Eighteen Models In an extensive empirical investigation into how automated software engineering tools process source code, researchers have demonstrated that large language models exhibit systematically higher confidence when predicting tokens in strongly typed programming languages than in dynamically typed scripting languages. The study, published in Automated Software Engineering by Zoe Kotti, Konstantina Dritsa, Diomidis Spinellis, and Panos Louridas, evaluated model perplexity across fourteen programming languages using eighteen open-weight language models. By analyzing a curated, balanced corpus of 2,254 source files harvested from 881 open-source GitHub projects, the authors established that languages enforcing formal type disciplines, most notably Java, Go, and C#, consistently yield lower perplexity scores than flexible scripting environments such as Perl, Ruby, and Shell. Across all eighteen evaluated model checkpoints, Shell emerged with universally high perplexity, while Java maintained consistently low perplexity. These empirical results illuminate how foundational programming language characteristics directly influence the certainty with which modern generative architectures anticipate programming sequences. The investigation addresses a critical methodological divide in artificial intelligence evaluation by examining intrinsic metrics rather than relying exclusively on downstream task performance. While conventional code generation benchmarks frequently depend on downstream execution measures such as Pass@k, BLEU scores, or CodeBLEU, these downstream evaluations prove computationally demanding, domain-specific, and vulnerable to noisy execution environments. In contrast, intrinsic statistical metrics, including perplexity, entropy, and mutual information, provide versatile, lightweight mathematical indicators of model uncertainty directly during next-token prediction. Perplexity quantifies how surprised a model is when encountering successive tokens given the preceding context, functioning mathematically as the exponentiated cross-entropy loss of the tokenized sequence. Previous empirical studies established that elevated perplexity correlates with higher error rates and increased hallucination risks in neural generation. By adopting perplexity as a primary diagnostic instrument, the research team established a standardized framework for quantifying generative confidence across development ecosystems without requiring custom execution sandboxes or test suites. To ensure rigorous evaluation without the confounding distortion of benchmark memorization or data leakage, the authors implemented a dataset construction protocol centered exclusively on copyleft repositories. Contemporary language models, including the original LLaMA foundation checkpoints, constructed their code pretraining corpora by querying Google BigQuery datasets of GitHub activity while filtering strictly for permissive licenses like Apache, BSD, and MIT. Capitalizing on this documented omission, the research team isolated projects licensed under GNU copyleft terms, specifically GPL-2.0, GPL-3.0, AGPL-3.0, LGPL-2.1, and LGPL-3.0, thereby minimizing overlap with the known training distributions of LLaMA and StarCoder 2. LLMs.title: Amazon Unleashes a Global AI Inference Gateway to Put Idle GPUs Back to Work - Kingy AI
LLMs.titleZh: Amazon Unleashes a Global AI Inference Gateway to Put Idle GPUs Back to Work - Kingy AI
LLMs.content: ## Amazon Tackles an Expensive AI Problem Imagine owning a fleet of expensive sports cars but leaving half of them parked while passengers queue for a ride. Sounds ridiculous, right? Something remarkably similar happens inside modern artificial intelligence infrastructure. Companies spend enormous amounts of money acquiring computing capacity. Yet distributing workloads efficiently across that infrastructure remains challenging. Amazon Web Services wants to change that. AWS has introduced the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway, a managed infrastructure technology that distributes AI inference requests across multiple computing clusters and geographical regions. The idea is refreshingly straightforward. Instead of allowing requests to accumulate behind overloaded infrastructure, AWS can redirect them toward suitable computing resources with available capacity. It isn’t another chatbot. Nor is it another enormous language model competing for benchmark supremacy. Instead, Amazon is improving the machinery that makes those products possible. For businesses operating artificial intelligence at scale, that distinction could make this announcement particularly important. ## The Hidden Challenge Behind Every AI Response Every time someone asks an AI assistant a question, something happens behind the scenes. Computers process the request, interpret the input, perform mathematical calculations, and generate an appropriate response. This process is called inference. Unlike training, which teaches an AI model to recognize patterns, inference puts that accumulated knowledge to work. The challenge grows when thousands of people submit requests simultaneously. Add document analysis, automated coding, image generation, and autonomous agents, and suddenly infrastructure management becomes considerably more complicated. Companies must accommodate fluctuating demand without purchasing unnecessarily large amounts of hardware. Unfortunately, predicting demand isn’t easy. A viral application can experience unexpected traffic. Corporate workloads may intensify during business hours. Automated agents can produce bursts of activity without much warning. Meanwhile, expensive computing resources elsewhere may remain underused. Amazon’s announcement addresses this imbalance rather than attempting to solve everything through additional hardware purchases. ## Meet the Global Inference Gateway The Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway introduces a centralized mechanism for coordinating inference workloads across registered HyperPod clusters. Applications communicate through one managed endpoint, even when the underlying infrastructure spans multiple regions. Think of it as an intelligent dispatcher. Instead of making every application decide where its request should go, the gateway handles that responsibility centrally. The underlying infrastructure can evolve without forcing developers to continuously rewrite application configurations. That separation matters. Infrastructure engineers can concentrate on expanding computing capacity and maintaining reliability. Application developers can focus on building useful products rather than managing complicated networking arrangements. The gateway doesn’t eliminate the need for infrastructure planning. Companies must still deploy models, configure permissions, and provision computing resources. However, Amazon removes some of the coordination headaches associated with distributed AI deployments. ## Why Traditional Infrastructure Can Waste Money Buying powerful GPUs represents only one part of the artificial intelligence spending equation. Companies also pay for electricity, networking, maintenance, engineering expertise, and supporting infrastructure. Underutilized hardware can therefore become a surprisingly expensive problem. Consider a fictional company operating AI workloads in Singapore and Tokyo. During a sudden increase in demand, its Singapore infrastructure becomes congested. ...

LLMs.title: Multilingual Emotion Profiling of Large Language Models Through Literary Texts and Persona Conditioning
LLMs.titleZh: Multilingual Emotion Profiling of Large Language Models Through Literary Texts and Persona Conditioning
LLMs.content: 2026 Volume 30 Issue 6 Pages 1866-1875 This paper examines whether multilingual prompt-and-text conditions materially alter large language model (LLM) emotion evaluation rather than merely rephrasing the same task. Using OpenRouter as a unified inference layer, we evaluated six contemporary LLMs under three full-language conditions (Japanese, English, and Traditional Chinese), three literary texts, four personas, and three repeated API calls per condition. Each completion rated four emotional dimensions — Interesting, Surprise, Sadness, and Anger — and provided a brief rationale. The design comprised 648 planned evaluations (6 models × 3 languages × 3 texts × 4 personas × 3 trials). The final combined dataset contained 648 valid records, comprising 631 original records and 17 replacement records obtained under a repair amendment registered after the main run and before the patch run. Descriptive summaries and preregistered ordinary least squares analyses with HC3 robust standard errors showed that text content was a major driver of scores, especially for Sadness and Anger. Simultaneously, model-language interactions were significant for all four emotions, indicating that the effect of the language condition varied substantially across models. English yielded the highest mean Interesting, Surprise, and Sadness scores, whereas Japanese yielded the highest mean Anger score. However, these aggregate patterns mask the strong model-specific contrasts. The findings show that multilingual literary evaluation is shaped by both the text itself and the model processing of its translation. This study contributes a multilingual literary emotion benchmark, a preregistered and repair-aware evaluation pipeline, and evidence that multilingual conditions are substantive experimental factors for LLM emotion profiling. AI Product.titleZh: The genAI gold rush puts legacy AI to the test
AI Product.content: - Premium Content It takes our newsroom weeks - if not months - to investigate and produce stories for our premium content. You can’t find them anywhere else. # The genAI gold rush puts legacy AI to the test For more than a decade, India-based AI company ShepHertz has built enterprise software powered by machine learning and computer vision. Among its products are facial recognition tools as well as software that monitors remote employees. But the generative AI boom has prompted it to rethink how it builds and sells AI. ShepHertz is in talks to raise US$10 million, its co-founder and CEO Siddhartha Chandurkar tells *Tech in Asia*. The funding will help it invest in GPU resources as it moves into the genAI and agent ecosystem. It will focus on bringing AI capabilities to devices such as drones, vehicles, and home appliances. The shift comes as genAI brings more money and customers into the market. VC investments in genAI firms reached US$35.5 billion in 2025, up from about US$2.8 billion in 2022. Meanwhile, US- and India-headquartered Fractal Analytics says “competition is very high” in the enterprise AI market. The 26-year-old firm was already positioned as an AI player before ChatGPT brought the technology into the mainstream. He says that when the company started, around 20% to 30% of his weekly meetings focused on AI, with discussions largely centered on data. Today, almost every meeting revolves around AI. > All the knowledge of the world is already collected, but how do I make it think more, reason more, and make it special-purpose? “About seven or eight years ago, we were evangelizing AI. Today, everyone knows about it, and we are telling them how to make it feasible,” says Sandeep Dutta, chief product officer of Fractal. For legacy AI companies, the challenge is proving that their expertise, products, and cost efficiencies can give them an edge as the tech becomes more widely accessible. ## Bringing AI closer to users Before generative AI became a multitrillion dollar industry, Fractal used machine learning and predictive analytics to help businesses make decisions. Its models could analyze customer purchase patterns. AI Product.content: # Hancom Takes AI Employee Platform 'Nomadian' to the US, Seeks AWS Sales Channel Integration South Korea's Hancom (030520.KQ) is taking aim at the US market with Nomadian, an AI workforce platform in which AI agents perform corporate tasks on users' behalf. The company has recruited a local business development specialist, discussed sales channels and commercialization plans with Amazon Web Services (AWS), and fleshed out a customer acquisition strategy aimed at entrepreneurs and small operators. Hancom said on Nov. 23 that it held a presentation on its US commercialization strategy for Nomadian at the Crowne Plaza hotel in Seattle on Nov. 16 (local time) and spent two days discussing cooperation with AWS. The event drew Eugene Kawamoto, AWS director of Amazon Bedrock and AI go-to-market (GTM), along with partners including VisualFeast, ClickIt and TaskUs, as well as local media. The most notable change is the staffing boost. Hancom has hired Bill Fanning as senior vice president (SVP) and head of US business development for Nomadian. Fanning has led new-product market entry for more than 15 years, previously serving as chief revenue officer (CRO) of AI recruiting platform Disway Global and founding Grilter, a recruiting candidate management solutions company. He also runs Talk Talent, a community of some 13,000 North American recruiting leaders. He will oversee Nomadian business development at the US subsidiary Hancom is in the process of establishing. Fanning pitched the ability to build and run an organization with AI before hiring actual employees as Nomadian's core competitive edge. The idea is to hand tasks such as customer response and project planning to an AI team, letting founders focus on growing the business. "What we're strategically focused on right now is the partnership with AWS," he said. "Based on Hancom's organizational foundation and capabilities, I'll make sure Nomadian delivers results quickly in the US." Nomadian is a platform in which AI agents carry out corporate work. In a three-dimensional (3D) virtual office, users can build an organization by deploying "Ara," an AI team leader, and 11 AI team members assigned by role and responsibility (R&R). When a task is assigned, Ara divides the work among team members — market and competitor research, marketing content creation, sales proposal writing and more. Users can check progress and review and edit reports and proposals produced with Hancom's 36 years of accumulated core document technology. The structure handles everything from task assignment to finished output on a single platform, with no need to switch between multiple AI tools. The AI team learns the user's working style and becomes more precisely tailored over time. Hancom plans to release a beta version next month and a global commercial version next March. The US commercialization strategy has three main prongs: building a local partner network, spreading the beta service, and acquiring customers through advertising. Hancom aims to secure partners including the US Small Business Development Center (SBDC), startup mentoring group SCORE, accelerators and university startup centers. The goal is 3 to 5 network partners before the beta service launches in December and 10 to 15 by next March. The beta service will also serve as a means of securing early customers. From December through February, Hancom plans to bring in 10,000 user companies each month, up to 30,000 in total. It will select 500 with the best results as "Nomadian 500," supporting them with prize money and mentoring, and use their use cases to attract additional customers. It will run advertising in major US cities to recruit beta service waitlist members. Cooperation with AWS is directly tied to securing sales channels. Nomadian is built on Amazon Bedrock, AWS's generative AI service. Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that lets users build generative AI applications and agents using foundation models from multiple AI companie...

Infra & Chips.content: Columns # Global AI industry faces 'Nvidia taper tantrum' As Nvidia tightens its purse strings following scrutiny of its vast AI investments, debt-dependent data center builders and the broader technology market face rising risks. **Ha Hyun-ock** *The author is an editorial writer at the JoongAng Ilbo.* The global AI industry faces an “Nvidia taper tantrum,” as investors fear that the company financing much of the sector could tighten its purse strings following former CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. Interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday that Nvidia would continue supporting and investing in the AI ecosystem but do so more systematically and with rigorous scrutiny, fueling the industry’s anxiety. The concern intensified after news broke of a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into Nvidia’s accounting practices. On Friday, the Nasdaq plunged 5.28 percent, erasing its gains for the year. Previously, customers raised money through their own resources, bonds or bank loans to build data centers and purchase chips. But Nvidia effectively became the AI sector’s central bank, supplying liquidity while assuming some clients’ financing risks; this helped finance infrastructure that would generate demand for Nvidia’s GPUs. Consequently, most of the AI ecosystem became dependent on the company’s support, creating a circular financing structure and rendering the industry vulnerable if its principal financial supporter changes course. Nvidia’s vendor financing extends through equity investments, purchase commitments and guarantees. The Wall Street Journal reported that the company’s investment portfolio, including stakes in companies that buy its chips, exceeds $100 billion, and Nvidia’s regulatory filings showed holdings worth more than $48 billion in eight publicly traded companies at the end of September. Cloud provider CoreWeave, in which Nvidia owns a 10 percent stake, exemplifies this relationship. In September 2025, Nvidia agreed to purchase $6.3 billion in CoreWeave computing capacity. By committing to buy unused capacity at qualifying data centers, the company reduced uncertainty involving its future revenue and helped CoreWeave obtain financing. It also reportedly agreed to guarantee $105 billion for SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary developing a data center to be leased by OpenAI, effectively backing the tenant’s rental obligations. Such deals expose Nvidia to financial obligations tied to whether customers can fill their facilities, generate cash and make payments on time. Nvidia also sought to attract Wall Street capital through an AI financing platform. In August, it announced plans for a $500 billion infrastructure investment consortium, signing memorandums of understanding with Apollo Global Management, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs and KKR. The initiative’s goal was to broaden financing beyond Nvidia itself. But no funds were deployed during its first three months, and reports suggested that one participant considered withdrawing after Huang’s departure. As Nvidia’s era of seemingly unlimited support approaches its end, the circular financing system that it helped construct faces mounting pressure. UBS analyst Tim Arcuri estimated that reduced Nvidia financing could rapidly withdraw more than $50 billion from the market. With borrowing costs already rising, the consequences could spread across the industry. Companies building data centers would face a double squeeze: more expensive financing and fewer guarantees or advance purchase commitments to reassure lenders. Warnings are multiplying. Former U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Gary Gensler told CNN on Nov. 16 that AI was in a bubble and predicted asset repricing and an economic slowdown before November 2028. His concern centers on enormous infrastructure spending, with some estimates putting annual AI infrastructure investment near $800 billion. Infra & Chips.content: # Nvidia Just Delivered Incredible Results. Buy This Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Instead If You’re Still Worried About the Semiconductor Giant’s Future **Nvidia** (NASDAQ:NVDA) delivered incredible results for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (which ended on Oct. 25) and, more importantly, raised its revenue guidance for fiscal 2028. Nvidia's financial performance and outlook should come as a relief for investors during a difficult time. The company's co-founder Jensen Huang recently resigned as CEO, and Nvidia is now in the hunt for a new one. However, comments from interim CEO Colette Kress on the latest earnings call clearly suggest that the company's growth prospects remain solid. *Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia.* Continue » Nvidia's revenue increased by 103% year-over-year last quarter to $115.8 billion, driven by a 110% jump in data center revenue. The company anticipates $130 billion in revenue for the current quarter, an improvement of 91% over the year-ago quarter. Even better, Nvidia has raised its fiscal 2028 revenue guidance to 75%, up from the prior expectation of 70%. So, I won't be surprised to see this artificial intelligence (AI) specialist go on a bull run once again. But if you're still on the sidelines about Nvidia's prospects, it may be a good idea to take a closer look at another semiconductor stock -- **ASML Holding** (NASDAQ:ASML). Here's why. Image source: Getty Images. ## Nvidia's improved guidance points to solid demand for advanced chips Nvidia's impressive data center growth in the previous quarter was driven by the incredible demand for its latest-generation Vera Rubin chip systems. The company noted that the Vera Rubin platform generated almost $20 billion in revenue last quarter, "making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history." The company noted that Rubin deployments will continue improving in 2027. Moreover, Nvidia management remarked that demand for its chips is outpacing supply. All this bodes well for ASML Holding, which manufactures the advanced chipmaking equipment that enables Nvidia to make the advanced Blackwell and Vera Rubin processors. Nvidia's Vera Rubin chip is built on a 3-nanometer (nm) process node, while the previous-generation Blackwell architecture, which remains in solid demand, is built on a 4-nm process node. These small process nodes are manufactured using extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, and ASML holds a near monopoly in this market.
